## The working approach

The current approach is to start with a small affordable Sobol pilot, then decide
whether to continue Sobol or try Bayesian optimization (BO). A typical pilot is
32 evaluations, counted inside the total budget. Reduce or omit it when objective
evaluations are extremely expensive or the candidate list is small and finite.
Stop when the stated target is reached. Otherwise consider how difficult it is to
find acceptable configurations, how costly each evaluation is, and whether a
surrogate can predict the response from the pilot.

Evaluate methods at comparable total time and quality, including initialization,
failed calls and controller overhead. Use withheld pilot observations for any
surrogate check, and keep final test data outside method selection. This is
workflow guidance, not an implemented automatic switch: study policy and budget
remain immutable during recovery, and there is no automatic pilot transfer to BO.
The open TODO is to **further explore a pilot-based selection rule**.

This approach draws on BO's motivation for expensive objectives [@frazier2018]
and the distinction between nominal and effective search dimension
[@bergstra2012]. Neither reference establishes the proposed pilot size or a
universal switching threshold. These five benchmark models do not validate a
selection rule across new problems.

## Reading the figures

The first figures describe the fixed and target experiments in `RESULTS.md`.
Model selectors expose all five problems. Colors identify random search, Sobol
and BO consistently in the target and checkpoint figures. Runtime colors identify
time components. Hover for exact values and use the
figure toolbar to zoom or download SVG. Printed output uses the saved SVG for
the selected view. The final three figures describe separate finite component
comparisons; they are not additional BO benchmark domains.

{{< include figures.qmd >}}

## Interpretation and limits

Use target difficulty and measured evaluation cost as separate inputs to method
selection. More physical detail or more nominal parameters need not make a given
target harder to reach. BO begins with Sobol initialization, so a run that stops
there says little about adaptive acquisition. Lower validation error can coexist
with worse test error, and short successful-only call counts must be read beside
censored runs.

The benchmark targets are development criteria, not global optima or scientific
accuracy standards. The larger models reuse the original data and splits. HYMOD
results are conditional on its initial stores; the inherited warmup cannot assure
equilibrium for the slowest reservoir. The single-diode module represents a proxy
for the plant hardware. Copper retains an unresolved source-unit multiplier.
Cached solar module-temperature observations in the BMI benchmark are unusable;
temperature-error diagnostics were withdrawn while the AC objective was retained.
The solar, wind and hybrid figures each state their distinct validation limits.

The working heuristic organizes an affordable decision process. Its pilot size,
surrogate diagnostics and economic switching criterion remain research questions.

## Provenance and reproduction

{{< include provenance.qmd >}}

Source: `examples/complex_models/results/RESULTS.md`, the `fixed` and
`target-2000` matrices, and `examples/open_chains/results`. Model sources,
forcing provenance and commands are documented in the corresponding example
READMEs. The report environment has a separate Pixi manifest and lockfile.

From the repository root:

```sh
pixi run -e examples python -m scripts.summarize_complex_models --target-directory target-2000
pixi run --manifest-path reports/model-search-results/pixi.toml render
```

The first command verifies the audited evidence and regenerates `RESULTS.md`.
The second verifies its plotted aggregates, generates figures and renders this
single HTML file. Figure data, code and input hashes accompany the source report.
